This study presents a novel time-series model called TD-PAR, a combination of the Poisson distribution and autoregression techniques with a focus on analyzing count data over time. The TD-PAR model includes both regular and seasonal components, making it an advanced counting model. Our research demonstrates that the TD-PAR model meets the requirements for a valid counting model, showing that it can be estimated effectively using maximum likelihood estimation. The TD-PAR model's capabilities are evaluated by conducting a series of forecasting tasks in comparison to existing models, indicating that it consistently delivers the most accurate results. A real-world application of the TD-PAR model is also demonstrated on a public dataset, showcasing its utility in predicting daily COVID-19 cases in a specific region.

While using photometry from stars to monitor the atmosphere may seem uncomplicated for optical astrophysics, achieving a precision of 0.01 for measuring the aerosol depth has been challenging. By taking wide-field photometry over a broad altitude range, the aerosol depth can be determined quickly, regardless of the system's absolute calibration, and even provides calibration as a by-product. Our team used extensive data from the FRAM telescope at the Pierre Auger Observatory and a similar telescope at the Cherenkov Telescope Array site to improve the precision of this technique to a precision of possibly 0.01. To accomplish this, we conducted precise laboratory measurements of the system's response to varying light intensities and spectra to counter the limitations of non-linear CCD detectors under observation conditions.

Numerous configurations of complex molecular systems can be effectively explored using molecular dynamics simulations, either by resolving the femtosecond timescale motions through classical mechanics or by employing Monte Carlo moves to sample new configurations directly. However, due to the exponential growth of possible configurations with molecule complexity, sampling the most promising configurations proves challenging. This challenge is particularly acute when conducting configurational sampling on complex systems like proteins, where resistance to conformational changes varies significantly among different parts of the molecule. To efficiently sample these configurations and mitigate the oscillations that can impede accurate temperature control, a modified Langevin dynamics approach has been developed. This method involves scaling the friction coefficient differently for kinetic and potential energy oscillations, thereby reducing the impact of friction on conformational changes and allowing more efficient configurational sampling. To utilize this approach effectively in biological systems, further research is needed on the optimal friction coefficient values for different molecular components and simulation conditions.

Human-generated descriptions are commonly used to train and evaluate image description systems, which are typically ranked based on how closely they match these descriptions. However, research suggests that these descriptions may not accurately reflect the images they correspond to, potentially leading to systems that generate descriptions mirroring existing data rather than describing images effectively. We propose a method to assess the quality of these descriptions, utilizing existing evaluation metrics and human feedback to improve description systems, which we demonstrate using data from two popular benchmarks: COCO and Conceptual Captions. Our findings indicate that these benchmarks contain numerous inaccuracies and biases, which affect evaluation outcomes and may influence generated descriptions. As a result, we advocate for a more rigorous assessment of image description data to ensure it is high-quality and useful for developing effective description systems.

Quantum conformal field theories in two dimensions can be described using perspective-free techniques, as seen in this work. A massless field of spin $s$ meets these requirements if its conformal dimension is $h = s$, under specific assumptions that hold true when the underlying manifold is a punctured complex plane. To verify this, we examine Euler-Arnold equations, drawing connections between conformal field theory, integrable representations, and classical field theory.

Predictions made by the QCD-based approach to forecast additional hadron spectra were reviewed. Since the confirmation of quark confinement in the late 1960s, the structure of quantum chromodynamics was understood. The classification of hadrons was predicted to mirror the representation structure of the symmetry group underlying the quark confinement mechanism. The underlying principle was applied to forecast additional baryon and meson spectra. The structure of the quark confinement mechanism was reviewed, along with the predicted hadron spectra based on different quark combinations. The forecasting criteria were also clarified, including the elimination of potentially duplicate spectrum predictions and the forecasting of hadron decay modes. The results were compared with existing experimental data and the current theoretical understanding of hadron spectra.

This article presents the SISO-OFDM and MISO-OFDM based IDED systems as alternatives to our previously proposed optimal wideband waveforming strategy in [1].
Fair-throughput and sum-throughput optimisation problems are defined and formulated.
By leveraging an algorithm that utilizes fixed points, we derive the optimal fair-throughput and sum-throughput values for SISO-OFDM and MISO-OFDM based IDED systems.

Integrating vast amounts of data from experiments in particle collisions is the purpose of the proposed framework, which is designed to fit models of particle distribution functions. The framework is constructed on a theoretical basis and is intended to ensure accuracy in the fitting process, particularly when fitting data from experiments involving collisions of protons and ions. Due to the complex nature of fitting PDF models, which involve multiple variables and sources of uncertainty, the proposed framework utilizes existing tools and techniques, including NNPDF, DSSK, and the PDF4TUN library, to implement a sophisticated fitting procedure. The proposed framework is capable of accurately determining the errors of PDF models, especially in regions where there is little experimental data, by incorporating the uncertainties of the fitting variables and the variables used to determine the data. The proposed framework also utilizes a novel approach to determine the errors of the PDF models at different points in time, which is a key improvement over existing tools. The proposed framework is further enhanced by incorporating a Monte Carlo simulation tool, DREAM, to accurately determine the errors of the PDF models and the variables used to determine the data. The proposed framework has the capability to fit multiple PDF models simultaneously to different sets of data, which is a significant advantage over existing tools. This study undertakes a linear analysis of a methane-air jet flame experiencing turbulence to determine how acoustic vibrations affect flame stability, while considering the complex interactions between flame dynamics, heat release, and flow fluctuations. To accurately predict flame response to acoustic forcing, it is crucial to account for heat released by the flame's fluctuations, which this study achieves using an active flame approach. Contrary to previous studies, the results reveal that acoustic forcing can suppress flame stability even when it delays flame oscillations, challenging the widely accepted idea that amplified acoustic pressure near the flame's base stabilizes flames. On the other hand, reduced pressure near the flame's base may lead to unstable flame behavior regardless of amplitude or frequency of acoustic forcing. These findings confirm the significance of considering the complex interactions between flame fluctuations, heat release, and flow fluctuations when analyzing flame response to acoustic forcing.

Nonlocal gravity theory is a classical generalization of Einstein's gravity theory. Based on an analogy with nonlocal electrodynamics, this new model involves a history-dependent relation that can be confirmed through data. The purpose of this paper is to modify nonlocal gravity theory so that the nonlocal aspect relates directly to observable properties. The reformulated theory is comparable to a fluid model, where the nonlocal aspect corresponds to viscosity. The underlying mechanics of this new model are examined, along with its applications and implications.

The Large Hadron Collider was designed to probe the fundamental structure of matter by colliding 7 TeV protons. While the majority of interactions have two or more particles in the final state, a small minority produce only one or two stable particles that can be detected. These minor events are statistically insignificant in terms of the cross-section, but potentially important in terms of their underlying physics. Despite their rarity, these events could potentially reveal new physics that might not be apparent through more frequent interactions. To fully exploit the LHC's research potential, a deeper analysis of these minor events is necessary, which may involve more sophisticated theoretical models and possibly even new detection strategies.

Observations of some variable X-ray sources within the Milky Way's center that have shown no outbursts in over a decade have led some researchers to suggest a significant population of stellar mass black holes in the region. A crucial aspect of the theory that these sources are actually black holes is the claim that neutron star binaries with low masses, which have long recurrence intervals, inevitably experience outbursts too infrequent to be detected within a 10-year period. This study examines the recurrence intervals of known low-mass neutron star binaries and challenges this notion by finding several systems with outburst periods exceeding a decade for the first time. Consequently, the data cannot be explained by a simple power law distribution of recurrence intervals and rejects the idea that all unsolved X-ray sources within the Milky Way's center are black holes.

Bipartite graphs depicting connections between distinct groups of objects have numerous practical applications, and their visualization often takes the form of a 2-tier layout where corresponding entities are aligned horizontally across two parallel lines, connected by lines representing relationships between them. The task of reducing edge crossings within these visualizations can be computationally intensive, yet might not always guarantee sufficiently low crossings levels to maintain the visualization's clarity. In contrast, an approach has been developed to remove edge crossings by splitting specific nodes, targeting the minimum number required to yield an edge-free (planar) drawing. The question of determining if an edge-free representation exists after breaking at most a specified number of nodes remains tractable in relation to that number.

As CPU frequencies continue to rise, power consumption and heat dissipation problems intensify. This research responds to this challenge by introducing HyperDegrade, a novel architecture that degrades high-frequency CPUs to operate effectively at much lower MHz ranges, while still achieving performance comparable to GHz frequencies. HyperDegrade's design involves a new pipelining strategy, a novel task manager, and an adaptive voltage scaling mechanism. The authors propose three different HyperDegrade configurations: HyperLite, HyperDual, and HyperQuad, which demonstrate significant performance gains over current GHz-based CPUs for lightweight, real-time, and general-purpose computing respectively. HyperDegrade's low-MHz variants outperform existing low-power LPDDR4x RAM by 10.5 times for lightweight computing, and HyperLite exhibits superior performance to a range of existing low-power CPUs for lightweight computing. HyperDegrade's code is available on GitHub at https://github.com/acmemb/HyperDegrade.

We introduce a new technique, called BigonPeel, that helps resolve mirror image issues in knot theory by altering a knot diagram in a way that doesn't affect its underlying knot type. This method uses an existing bigon to remove a crossing in a knot diagram without introducing new bigons or altering existing ones. We demonstrate how BigonPeel can be used to show that the knot concurrence invariant is skew to the knot rotation invariant. Additionally, we utilize BigonPeel to prove a new statement regarding the rotation invariant and the mirror image invariant being linearly dependent for a wide range of knot classes, specifically those with distinct sharp knots and their shallow reflections.

In a collaborative robot network with limited capabilities, we examine the process of achieving the same through coordination and decision-making on multiple tasks. A strategy is proposed where tasks are learned through communication and computation on the network graph. We demonstrate that a linear set of actions is sufficient for the robots to converge on the optimal action for each task on a regular graph. A theoretical model has been established to predict the learning rate of the robots on the network. A key contribution of the research is the discovery that the proposed strategy results in the robots learning the same information on the spectrum of the graph laplacian. The proposed approach has been applied to a variety of regular graph topologies and their performance has been compared.

In our study, we demonstrated how both a group that operates on a set in a recurring manner and a diagonal group are effectively incorporated into the wreath products under their combined, or product action, utilizing the Cartesian Breakdown approach.

The upgrade of advanced LIGO and Virgo interferometric gravitational wave detectors aims to enhance their sensitivity for low-frequency signals. However, improving their sensitivity at higher frequencies is challenging due to the constant source of noise from optical resonances within the mirror materials. Overcoming this limitation is crucial for detecting gravitational waves generated by binary neutron star mergers. We propose a novel interferometer design, the sloshing-Sagnac topology, which uses multiple mirrors and beam splitters to counteract the resonant noise. By utilizing two non-interfering beam cavities within the mirror, this design can potentially reduce the effects of resonant noise at high frequencies without introducing additional sources of noise from additional optical resonances. Initial simulations indicate that this enhanced design could improve the sensitivity of future gravitational wave detectors by as much as 5 times around 100 Hz of frequency, with minimal additional technical complexity.

Recent large-scale MIMO systems are considered an exciting development, capable of providing rapid data transfer in crowded environments. As a result of their substantial size, MIMO arrays are susceptible to blockage, which can lead to significant variations in signal reach. Researchers have noted that in crowded areas with many users, partially or fully blocked areas without user coverage are a common occurrence. Such areas with reduced or no coverage are referred to as visibility regions and can be either fully or partially obstructed. Partially obstructed regions may be served by arrays located near the ground, whereas fully obstructed regions cannot be reached by any arrays. Understanding the distribution of visibility regions is crucial for designing efficient protocols and optimizing base station capabilities. With numerous possible configurations, determining a precise formula for the average visibility region size is complex. However, researchers have established an estimate, stating that in crowded areas with similar signal strength reach for all users, the average fully obstructed regions are extremely small, only occupying a tiny fraction of the total area, specifically 1 percent, when the coverage area of each array is highly variable, and 0.01 percent when the coverage areas are similar in size.

Neural text generation models have revolutionized language processing but have been outperformed by traditional n-gram models in certain applications. To improve neural models and explore their potential uses in language modeling, we design a novel architecture that learns from the differences between n-gram and neural models, drawing on the concept of residual learning. We conduct experiments using various n-gram models, find that certain n-gram models excel in specific contexts, and observe notable improvements with the proposed architecture. Our best results using a bigram model surpass the current state of the art in a key measurement, suggesting future research could focus on combining n-gram and neural models through residual learning.

This investigation seeks to examine the effectiveness of using optical character recognition technology in accurately capturing election results, which are often publicized with scanned images of paper ballots, and draws on a dataset of 100,000 manually entered votes from a local election.

A simplified computer model is used to investigate various global atmospheric circulation patterns with the aim of understanding the underlying causes and conditions that lead to different circulation states on terrestrial planets with thin atmospheres. By adjusting key parameters such as angular momentum, viscosity, and rotation rates, multiple scenarios are explored and the resulting circulation patterns are mapped in a two-dimensional graphical format to identify patterns that develop under various conditions. The results show that circulation patterns on thin-atmosphere planets are primarily influenced by the planet's rotation rate and atmospheric stability, and that an excess of angular momentum can lead to extremely fast atmospheric circulation patterns or slower, more complex patterns of circulation, and even separate fast and slow circulation layers on different parts of the planet.
This study formulates integral representations of the reciprocal gamma function, partially inspired by the Wallis formula, and demonstrates its connection to a specific product notation.

Researchers have developed a new theoretical framework called hydrodynamic theories, which aims to describe the dynamics of quantum many-body systems in real and momentum spaces. This paper extends previous hydrodynamic methods by introducing a random phase-space approach that accounts for fluctuations of the field operator, thereby enabling the inclusion of higher-order corrections in perturbation series. The authors achieve this innovative framework through a novel derivation from a hydrodynamic action that includes both real and momentum-space density fluctuations, which they term as "condensate" and "quasi-condensate" fluctuations. This random phase-space hydrodynamic theory is applicable to interacting Bose gases and overcomes limitations of current hydrodynamic models, which only describe linear response phenomena. The authors further demonstrate the theoretical values of the second-order cumulant of the quasi-condensate fluctuation and the third-order susceptibility of the system in the new framework.

Deep Neural Networks have become incredibly complex, leading to a recognition that the current single-source architecture may not be the most effective way to design and train them, especially given the significant energy and computational costs involved. This survey introduces the Instructor-Student architecture, a novel framework that decouples the training process by incorporating multiple sources of knowledge, drawing upon the expertise of an experienced instructor network and feedback from a student network. A key advantage of this architecture is the potential to leverage existing pre-trained models as instructors, eliminating the need for costly training from scratch. Furthermore, the survey explores the various applications and purposes of the instructor and student networks, as well as the multiple roles the instructor can play in teaching the student through knowledge sharing, regularization, and optimization. A comprehensive discussion on the design and optimization strategies for both the instructor and student networks is also provided, including knowledge updating algorithms, optimization algorithms, and performance evaluation guidelines. With its wide-ranging applications in computer science, engineering, and economics, the Instructor-Student architecture is poised to revolutionize the design and training of deep neural networks, making them more efficient, effective, and accessible for use in various tasks and domains.

We introduce a new efficient algorithm that uses a brief representation of conditional probabilities in graphical models, which we've termed as "brief functions". This brief function notation allows us to quickly compute the most probable explanation for exact MPE problems and efficiently solves constrained optimisation problems by adding a small constant term to the potential function. The brief function algorithm outperforms the current state-of-the-art method, SDD-SG, by an average of 10 times faster MPE computation and reduces the gap in constrained optimisation problem solving to a small constant.

Recently introduced is a higher rank algebra known as the centralizer algebra $Z_n(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$ for the special Lie algebra $\mathfrak{sl}_{n+1}$. The centralizer $Z_{n+1}(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$ is identified as a deformation of the classical Weyl algebra. The centralizer $Z_n(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$ is found to be isomorphic with the Racah algebra $W(n+1)$. The centralizer $Z_{n+1}(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$'s Hilbert-Poincar\'e series is determined.

The paired-permutation test in NLP systems has long relied on testing the statistical significance of differences in performance. This test aims to verify that observed discrepancies aren't simply coincidental. Despite the importance of accurate results, paired-permutation testing is often criticized for its slow performance due to the time-consuming process of sampling permutations. In response, we've developed a more efficient paired-permutation testing method that uses a precise algorithm to calculate the exact rank of the statistic in its distribution. This precise algorithm allows us more flexibility to explore alternative structured test statistics that incorporate knowledge of the ranking. We've also expanded our options to include all possible structured rankings or limits on the maximum gap between the desired and actual rankings. Our precise algorithm yields significantly better results compared to existing approaches and takes significantly less time to compute.

Our research examined the connection between initial anisotropic geometry and anisotropic flow within a multiphase transport model, specifically for 200 GeV Au+Au and Cu+Cu collisions. Contrary to elliptical anisotropy $\vett{\epsilon}$, our results showed that triangular anisotropy $\vett{\epsilon}_3$ cannot be accurately described using a fixed anisotropic initial geometry, even when considering fluctuations in the particle density. However, once we accounted for non-equilibrium emergent anisotropies resulting from partonic coherence in the heavy ion collision process, the model demonstrated significant improvement in reproducing Adare et al.'s $v_3/\vett{\epsilon}_3$ data for Au+Au collisions at 200 GeV. Moreover, we observed that non-equilibrium anisotropic effects in the heavy quark potential couldn't significantly impact $v_3$ following the heavy ion collision, as indicated by our results showing a lack of significant change in $v_3$ even after introducing varying non-equilibrium anisotropic distributions in the heavy quark potential.

This study adapts the Poisson Basket Merging (PMBM) filter to utilize a partially grid-based origin model, offering a precise understanding of Poisson parameters lambda and beta. The revised algorithm demonstrates its potential in assessing the value of beta by using partially sampled data. A partially grid-based origin model with varying lambda values is employed to evaluate the PMBM filter's performance in diverse settings. A simple sensor management strategy is also proposed, using the s-value from the PMBM filter to determine the activation or deactivation of sensors. The optimal sensor configuration is determined through further analysis of the approach's reliability in dense sensor networks.

The dynamics of soccer games can be unpredictable, making it challenging to execute set pieces effectively. Despite the importance of these situations, there is a lack of data in the soccer game dataset, which complicates the problem for machine learning models. This research addresses this challenge by introducing an enhanced action called the "Swerving Shot" that aims to deceive the opponent through deception, which may be particularly useful in critical set piece situations. To investigate the effectiveness of this new action, a reinforcement learning framework was employed to learn the optimal strategy for executing the Swerving Shot, which resulted in higher goal expectations compared to the existing shot action in the dataset.

The development of optical fibers has enabled the creation of large-scale, multi-point Laser Doppler Velocimetry (LDV) systems. This technology allows multiple points to be measured simultaneously using a single laser source. In this system, multiple optical fibers carry the measurement signal to a single detection unit, making it possible to obtain two-dimensional velocity distributions. Such a system can be used to study complex flow phenomena, but its setup is complex and costly. Alternatively, multiple single-point LDV systems can be used to obtain two-dimensional measurements, but this approach is time-consuming and cumbersome. In contrast, our multi-point LDV system with a single-distance measurement is a simple and cost-effective approach that can be used to study various flow phenomena. It is particularly useful for researching large-scale flows in areas with limited access, such as in aerospace engineering. In this research, we used a multi-point LDV system with a single-distance measurement to investigate the flow around an airfoil and obtained accurate two-dimensional velocity measurements. This technique can be applied to research the flow behavior in various geometries and areas with complex optical interference issues.

We provide explicit definitions for the spectral and orbital stability of solitary waves in a model that includes a Klein-Gordon equation and an anharmonic oscillator. We also conduct a comprehensive analysis of the linearized equation's spectrum at the solitary wave state.

In experiments involving particle collisions, light particles with low masses can go unnoticed if they do not interact with detectors through significant processes such as decay or missing energy. Despite this, theoretical models suggest that some lowmass particles might leave no trail in detectors despite potentially being present. A class of models where a lowmass particle takes the place of a standard model particle in a decay process is of particular interest. Researchers examining $B$ decay data from the Belle II experiment can look for instances where this lowmass particle might be substituting for a pion in decay sequences. Although statistical analysis may not detect this particle if it leaves no signal in the Belle II detector, data from the LHC could potentially fill this gap if the particle interacts with a high-energy particle and leaves no trail. If this type of particle exists and meets certain mass requirements, it might also explain phenomena observed in experiments involving atomic collisions. To search for this particle, researchers can examine data from $B$ decay sequences where a lowmass particle is believed to be substituting for a pion. This investigation involves analyzing multiple data points from the Belle II experiment and drawing comparisons with results from a corresponding analysis of LHC data. If the particle meets the predicted mass range, researchers can use a theoretical model to better understand its properties and behavior. If the particle's mass is too low to be detected through decay processes, it might be difficult to confirm its existence through future experiments involving high-energy collisions. The increasing use of sophisticated contextualized language models for generating text has created challenges in detecting altered semantics, particularly when identifying instances where the generated text conveys a different meaning than the original input. This research paper investigates the effectiveness of these contextualized language models in fulfilling this role and presents valuable insights and findings. Our results demonstrate that contextualized language models can accurately identify situations where the semantics of generated text have changed but may also overfit to specific data and exhibit inconsistent performance when confronted with slang, idioms, and ambiguous words. These complexities highlight the necessity for training these models on a diverse range of semantic alteration instances to ensure they can effectively identify altered semantics in real-world scenarios.

Active galactic nuclei (AGNs), containing accreting black holes at their center, offer a unique laboratory for investigating black hole mass and spin through the analysis of electromagnetic spectra. While a majority of AGNs feature masses less than $10^{9}$ times that of the sun, some exceptionally luminous quasars have been discovered with masses exceeding $10^{10}$ solar masses. The spin of the black hole plays a crucial role in powering the intense radiation observed in these systems, with higher spin values leading to more efficient energy production. However, certain theoretical models suggest that even when a black hole has a large impact on its environment, its own internal properties might not be fully determined by how it interacts with that environment. In particular, a hole with a large effect on its surroundings might appear smaller and less massive than it actually is. This phenomenon, known as the "mass-inflation problem," poses a challenge for the formation of extremely massive black holes at the centers of quasars with low spin rates. To address this issue, we examined a sample of 26 quasars with extremely large black hole masses, analyzing how their spin parameters and masses are correlated. Our results indicate that despite the uncertainties involved, these quasars with exceptionally large black hole masses are more likely to have high spin rates, similar to those found in a previous study of a larger quasars sample.
